from pathlib import Path
r = PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
out = Path('tmp/pdfs')
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
print('PAGES', len(r.pages))
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 (out/f'page-{i:02}.txt').write_text(t)
 texts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+t)
(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n'.join(texts))
print('\\n'.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful question: when architectural equivariance and data augmentation yield the same optimization dynamics, and when their stability differs. Comparing both approaches within a shared parameter space makes this distinction precise.

Under suitable differentiability assumptions, Lemma 4 and Propositions 1–2 provide sound group-averaging identities. These establish agreement of the augmented and projected gradients on E, equality of stationary-point sets within E, and separation of tangential and normal Hessian blocks.

The presentation is largely self-contained, with explicit representations, supporting proofs, and detailed architectural descriptions. Experiments cover three symmetry settings with 30 repetitions; Appendix E.2 additionally holds the architecture and dataset fixed while varying the group. A code link and computational budgets are provided.

Remark 1 and Section 6 appropriately acknowledge the infinite-augmentation idealization and the local scope of the analysis. The public MNIST and synthetic datasets present no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The experiments do not establish the claimed consistent instability of E in Section 5.1. AUG uses finite, randomly sampled transformations, whose gradient noise can produce departures from E even when the exact augmented flow is attracting. Figures 1 and 6 measure departure without separating stochastic forcing from deterministic amplification. Controlled perturbation experiments, normal-Hessian measurements, or exact group averaging would be needed to support this interpretation; exact averaging is particularly feasible for the four-element rotation group.

Proposition 3 is not proved at its stated generality: its proof assumes positive-definite Hessians, whereas strict local minima can have singular Hessians. Furthermore, R_eqv(A)=R(Π_E A) is constant along E-perpendicular directions, so its strict minima must explicitly be defined relative to E. The subsequent assertion that the Hessian spectrum completely determines stability also requires qualification when zero eigenvalues occur. These are consequential distinctions for neural networks with parameter degeneracies.

The regularity assumptions are insufficiently specified. Assumptions 1–3 impose symmetry but do not justify the Hessians, differentiation under expectations, or the quadratic Taylor remainder used in Section 4.2. The experiments use leaky ReLUs, so global smoothness cannot simply be presumed. The analysis needs explicit regularity conditions and a clear account of its applicability at activation boundaries.

Equation (7) incorrectly equates augmentation risk with the risk of the averaged prediction. For squared loss, augmented predictions +1 and −1 with target 0 give augmentation risk 1, while their averaged prediction has risk 0. Convexity generally yields an inequality, not equality. Although Lemma 4 does not depend on this error, the stated relationship to feature averaging is mathematically incorrect.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for the central experiment: the manuscript does not specify the actual N_aug, batch size, or numerical precision. These directly affect the small departures being interpreted as instability. Normalization is also described inconsistently: Section 5 specifies layer normalization, while Appendix D.3 describes batch normalization for ROT.

The originality and demonstrated significance are limited. The nonlinear-MLP formulation is useful, but most conclusions after Lemma 4 follow from standard properties of invariant objectives. The paper supplies neither a characterization of transverse curvature in the studied networks nor evidence connecting the observed parameter drift to training loss or prediction equivariance. Consequently, the claimed practical implications are stronger than the demonstrated understanding.
